newsitem.title: USA: Court rejects death row inmate's appeal for stay.
newsitem.headline: Court rejects death row inmate's appeal for stay.

text.p: An appeals court on Friday rejected a petition for a stay of execution by convicted murderer Coleman Wayne Gray, who is scheduled to die next Wednesday.
The three-judge panel of the the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals in Richmond, Virginia ruled unanimously and without comment. The court also denied Gray permission to submit a further appeal.
Gray, 39, is scheduled to die by lethal injection on Wednesday in the Greensville Correctional Facility in Jarratt, Virginia for the May 1985 murder of grocery store manager Richard McClelland.
In a telephone interview with Reuters from his prison cell on death row on Thursday, Gray insisted that he was not the murderer and said he was the victim of false testimony.

"I believe we have the best judicial system in the world but sometimes mistakes are made and mistakes were made here. Now that it's been shown that false testimony was given, I hope the system will do the right thing," he said, speaking of his petition -- which was subsequently turned down on Friday.
Gray is left with only two legal recourses -- an appeal to the Supreme Court, which has already rejected his appeal once, and a bid for clemency to Virginia Gov. George Allen.

Gray was convicted largely on the testimony of co-defendant Melvin Tucker of robbing and abducting McClelland and shooting him six times in the back of the head, despite his pleas for mercy. Gray says Tucker was the trigger man.

At the penalty stage of the trial, Tucker testified that Gray bragged of having committed two other murders -- the 1984 killings of Lisa Sorrell and her three-year-old daughter Shanta -- in much the same way he murdered McClelland.

In an affidavit filed this week to the Court of Appeals in Richmond, Tucker recanted that testimony, saying he was forced to perjure himself by the prosecution to avoid the death penalty himself. But Tucker still maintains that Gray killed McClelland.

"The story I gave about Gray looking in the newspaper and referring to a picture of the Sorrells was a lie. My testimony concerning Coleman Gray telling me that he killed the Sorrell woman and child was a lie," Tucker said in his affidavit.

The Commonwealth of Virginia said in response that the defence had not raised any new arguments. "Such a recantation of penalty-stage testimony is incapable of constituting 'clear and convincing evidence' that Gray is not guilty of capital murder," the state said.
Gray said in the interview with Reuters that he believed in heaven and hell and hoped his spirit would go to heaven and "reside with Jesus."
He said he was convinced the state of Virginia was determined to put him to death rather than face up to questions about the way his case was handled.
"They would rather see me dead than have these injustices exposed. I still hope they will do the right thing," he said.
